The honour of constancy and resolution in the way of duty will be a lasting honour; and those that are manifest to God, will be manifest in the consciences of those about them. [2.] As an instance of the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees, who paid their respect to them. Note, Carnal people can easily honour the memories of faithful ministers that are dead and gone, because they do not reprove them, nor disturb them, in their sins. Dead prophets are <hi type="italic">seers that see not,</hi> and those they can bear well enough; they do not torment them, as the living witnesses do, that bear their testimony <hi type="italic">viva voce—with a living voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.11.10">Rev. xi. 10</reference>. They can pay respect to the writings of the dead prophets, which tell them what they <hi type="italic">should</hi> be; but not the reproofs of the living prophets, which tell them what they <hi type="italic">are.</hi> <hi type="italic">Sit divus, modo non sit vivus—Let there be saints; but let them not be living here.</hi> The extravagant respect which the church of Rome pays to the memory of saints departed, especially the martyrs, dedicating days and places to their names, enshrining their relics, praying to them, and offering to their images, while they make themselves drunk with the blood of the saints of their own day, is a manifest proof that they not only <hi type="italic">suc</hi>ceed, but <hi type="italic">ex</hi>ceed, the scribes and Pharisees in a counterfeit hypocritical religion, which builds the prophets' tombs, but hates the prophets' doctrine. <div eID="gen23474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23475" type="x-p"/> (2.) They protested against the murder of them (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.30">v. 30</reference>); <hi type="italic">If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them.</hi> They would never have consented to the silencing of Amos, and the imprisonment of Micaiah, to the putting of Hanani in the stocks, and Jeremiah in the dungeon, to the stoning of Zechariah, the mocking of all the messengers of the Lord, and the abuses put upon his prophets; no, not they, they would sooner have lost their right hands than have done any such thing. <hi type="italic">What, is thy servant a dog?</hi> And yet they were at this time plotting to murder Christ, <hi type="italic">to whom all the prophets bore witness.</hi> They think, if they had lived in the days of the prophets, they would have heard them gladly and obeyed; and yet they rebelled against the light that Christ brought into the world. But it is certain, a Herod and an Herodias to John the Baptist, would have been an Ahab and a Jezebel to Elijah. Note, The deceitfulness of sinners' hearts appears very much in this, that, while they go down the stream of the sins of their own day, they fancy they should have swum against the stream of the sins of the former days; that, if they had had other people's opportunities, they should have improved them more faithfully; if they had been in other people's temptations, they should have resisted them more vigorously; when yet they improve not the opportunities they have, nor resist the temptations they are in. We are sometimes thinking, if we had lived when Christ was upon earth, how constantly we would have followed him; we would not have despised and rejected him, as they then did; and yet Christ in his Spirit, in his word, in his ministers, is still no better treated. <div eID="gen23475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23476" type="x-p"/> 2. Their enmity and opposition to Christ and his gospel, notwithstanding, and the ruin they were bringing upon themselves and upon that generation thereby, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.31-Matt.23.33">v. 31-33</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen23476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23477" type="x-p"/> (1.) The indictment proved; <hi type="italic">Ye are witnesses against yourselves.</hi> Note, Sinners cannot hope to escape the judgment of Christ for want of proof against them, when it is easy to find them witnesses against themselves; and their very pleas will not only be overruled, but turned to their conviction, and <hi type="italic">their own tongues</hi> shall be made to <hi type="italic">fall upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen23477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23478" type="x-p"/> [1.] By their own confession, it was the great wickedness of their forefathers, to kill the prophets; so that they knew the fault of it, and yet were themselves guilty of the same fact. Note, They who condemn sin in others, and yet allow the same or worse in themselves, are of all others most inexcusable, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.32-Rom.2.1">Rom. i. 32-ii. 1</reference>. They knew they ought not to have been partakers with persecutors, and yet were the followers of them. Such self-contradictions now will amount to self-condemnations in the great day. Christ puts another construction upon their building of the tombs of the prophets than what they intended; as if by beautifying their graves they justified their murderers (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.48">Luke xi. 48</reference>), for they persisted in the sin. <div eID="gen23478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23479" type="x-p"/> [2.] By their own confession, these notorious persecutors were their ancestors; <hi type="italic">Ye are the children of them.</hi> They meant no more than that they were their children by blood and nature; but Christ turns it upon them;, that they were so by spirit and disposition; <hi type="italic">You are of those fathers, and their lusts you will do.</hi> They are, as you say, <hi type="italic">your</hi> fathers, and you <hi type="italic">patrizare—take after your fathers;</hi> it is the sin that runs in the blood among you. <hi type="italic">As your fathers did, so do ye,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Acts vii. 51</reference>. They came of a persecuting race, were <hi type="italic">a seed of evil doers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa. i. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">risen up in their fathers' stead,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.32.14">Num. xxxii. 14</reference>. Malice, envy, and cruelty, were bred in the bone with them, and they had formerly espoused it for a principle, to <hi type="italic">do as their fathers did,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer. xliv. 17</reference>. And it is observable here (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.30">v. 30</reference>) how careful they are to mention the relation; "They were <hi type="italic">our</hi> fathers, that killed the prophets, and they were men in honour and power, whose sons and successors we are." If they had detested the wickedness of their ancestors, as they ought to have done, they would not have been so fond to call them <hi type="italic">their fathers;</hi> for it is no credit to be akin to persecutors, though they have ever so much dignity and dominion. <div eID="gen23479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23480" type="x-p"/> (2.) The sentence passed upon them. Christ here proceeds, <div eID="gen23480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23481" type="x-p"/> [1.] To give them up to sin as irreclaimable (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">v. 32</reference>); <hi type="italic">Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers.</hi> If Ephraim be joined to idols, and hate to be reformed, <hi type="italic">let him alone. He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.</hi> Christ knew they were now contriving his death, and in a few days would accomplish it; "Well," saith he, "go on with your plot, take your curse, walk in the way of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, and see what will come of it. <hi type="italic">What thou doest, do quickly.</hi> You will but fill up the measure of guilt, which will then overflow in a deluge of wrath." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There is a measure of sin to be filled up, before utter ruin comes upon persons and families, churches and nations. God will bear long, but the time will come when he can <hi type="italic">no longer forbear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.44.22">Jer. xliv. 22</reference>. We read of the measure of the Amorites that was to be filled (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen. xv. 16</reference>), of the <hi type="italic">harvest</hi> of the earth <hi type="italic">being ripe for the sickle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.15-Rev.14.19">Rev. xiv. 15-19</reference>), and of sinners <hi type="italic">making an end to deal treacherously,</hi> arriving at a full stature in treachery, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Children fill up the measure of their fathers' sins whey they are gone, if they persist in the same or the like. That national guilt which brings national ruin is made up of the sin of many in several ages, and in the successions of societies there is a score going on; for God justly visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children that tread in the steps of it. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Persecuting Christ, and his people and ministers, is a sin that fills the measure of a nation's guilt sooner than any other. This was it that brought wrath without remedy upon the fathers (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2 Chron. xxxvi. 16</reference>), and wrath to the utmost upon the children too, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 16</reference>. This was that fourth transgression, of which, when added to the other three, the Lord <hi type="italic">would not turn away the punishment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3 Amos.1.6 Amos.1.9 Amos.1.11 Amos.1.13">Amos i. 3, 6, 9, 11, 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It is just with God to give those up to their own heart's lusts, who obstinately persist in the gratification of them. Those who will run headlong to ruin, let the reins be laid on their neck, and it is the saddest condition a man can be in on this side hell. <div eID="gen23481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23482" type="x-p"/> [2.] He proceeds to give them up to ruin as irrecoverable, to a personal ruin in the other world (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.33">v. 33</reference>); <hi type="italic">Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?</hi> These are strange words to come from the mouth of Christ, into whose lips grace was poured. But he can and will speak terror, and in these words he explains and sums up the <hi type="italic">eight</hi> woes he had denounced against the scribes and Pharisees. <div eID="gen23482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23483" type="x-p"/> Here is, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their description; <hi type="italic">Ye serpents.</hi> Doth Christ call names? Yes, but this doth not warrant us to do so. He infallibly knew what was in man, and knew them to be subtle as serpents, cleaving to the earth, feeding on dust; they had a specious outside, but were within malignant, had poison under their tongues, the seed of the old serpent. They were a <hi type="italic">generation of vipers;</hi> they and those that went before them, they and those that joined with them, were a generation of envenomed, enraged, spiteful adversaries to Christ and his gospel. They loved to be called of men, <hi type="italic">Rabbi, rabbi,</hi> but Christ calls them <hi type="italic">serpents</hi> and <hi type="italic">vipers;</hi> for he gives men their true characters, and delights to put contempt upon the proud. <div eID="gen23483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23484" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Their doom. He represents their condition as very sad, and in a manner desperate; <hi type="italic">How can ye escape the damnation of hell?</hi> Christ himself preached hell and damnation, for which his ministers have often been reproached by those that care not to hear of it. Note, 1. The damnation of hell will be the fearful end of all impenitent sinners. This doom coming from Christ, was more terrible than coming from all the prophets and ministers that ever were, for he is the Judge, into whose hands the keys of hell and death are put, and his saying they were damned, made them so. 2. There is a way of escaping this damnation, this is implied here; some are <hi type="italic">delivered from the wrath to come.</hi> 3. Of all sinners, those who are of the spirit of the scribes and Pharisees, are least likely to escape this damnation; for repentance and faith are necessary to that escape; and how will <hi type="italic">they</hi> be brought to these, who are so conceited of themselves, and so prejudiced against Christ and his gospel, as they were? How could they be healed and saved, who could not bear to have their wound searched, nor the balm of Gilead applied to it? Publicans and harlots, who were sensible of their disease and applied themselves to the Physician, were more likely to escape the damnation of hell than those who, though they were in the high road to it, were confident they were in the way to heaven.
entries.a3dc27b5c9f37dc130880767f31307263a790092: <div eID="gen23484" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of the Pharisees; The Guilt and Doom of Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen23485" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> Wherefore, behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes: and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of them ye shall kill and crucify; and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of them shall ye scourge in your synagogues, and persecute <hi type="italic">them</hi> from city to city: <hi type="super">35</hi> That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar. <hi type="super">36</hi> Verily I say unto you, All these things shall come upon this generation. <hi type="super">37</hi> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under <hi type="italic">her</hi> wings, and ye would not! <hi type="super">38</hi> Behold, your house is left unto you desolate. <hi type="super">39</hi> For I say unto you, Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> he that cometh in the name of the Lord. <div eID="gen23485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23486" type="x-p"/> We have left the blind leaders fallen into the ditch, under Christ's sentence, into the damnation of hell; let us see what will become of the blind followers, of the body of the Jewish church, and particularly Jerusalem. <div eID="gen23486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23487" type="x-p"/> I. Jesus Christ designs yet to try them with the means of grace; <hi type="italic">I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes.</hi> The connection is strange; "<hi type="italic">You are a generation of vipers,</hi> not likely to <hi type="italic">escape the damnation of hell;</hi>" one would think it should follow, "Therefore you shall never have a prophet sent to you any more;" but no, "<hi type="italic">Therefore I will send unto you prophets,</hi> to see if you will yet at length be wrought upon, or else to leave you inexcusable, and to justify God in your ruin." It is therefore ushered in with a note of admiration, behold! Observe, <div eID="gen23487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23488" type="x-p"/> 1. It is Christ that sends them; <hi type="italic">I send.</hi> By this he avows himself to be God, having power to gift and commission prophets. It is an act of kingly office; he sends them as ambassadors to treat with us about the concerns of our souls. After his resurrection, he made this word good, when he said, <hi type="italic">So send I you,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.21">John xx. 21</reference>. Though now he appeared mean, yet he was entrusted with this great authority. <div eID="gen23488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23489" type="x-p"/> 2. He sends them to the Jews first; "I send them to <hi type="italic">you.</hi>" They began at Jerusalem; and, wherever they went, they observed this rule, to make the first tender of gospel grace <hi type="italic">to the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">Acts xiii. 46</reference>. <div eID="gen23489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23490" type="x-p"/> 3. Those he sends are called <hi type="italic">prophets, wise men,</hi> and <hi type="italic">scribes,</hi> Old-Testament names for New-Testament officers; to show that the ministers sent to them now should not be inferior to the prophets of the Old Testament, to Solomon the wise, or Ezra the scribe. The extraordinary ministers, who in the first ages were divinely inspired, were as the prophets commissioned immediately from heaven; the ordinary settled ministers, who were then, and continue in the church still, and will do to the end of time, are as the wise men and scribes, to guide and instruct the people in the things of God. Or, we may take the apostles and evangelists for the prophets and wise men, and the pastors and teachers for the scribes, <hi type="italic">instructed to the kingdom of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.52">ch. xiii. 52</reference>); for the office of a scribe was honourable till the men dishonoured it. <div eID="gen23490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23491" type="x-p"/> II. He foresees and foretels the ill usage that his messengers would meet with among them; "<hi type="italic">Some of them ye shall kill and crucify,</hi> and yet I will send them." Christ knows beforehand how ill his servants will be treated, and yet sends them, and appoints them their measure of sufferings; yet he loves them never the less for his thus exposing them, for he designs to glorify himself by their sufferings, and them after them; he will counter-balance them, though not prevent them. Observe, <div eID="gen23491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23492" type="x-p"/> 1. The cruelty of these persecutors; <hi type="italic">Ye shall kill and crucify them.</hi> It is no less than the blood, the life-blood, that they thirst after; their lust is not satisfied with any thing short of their destruction, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.9">Exod. xv. 9</reference>. They killed the two James's, crucified Simon the son of Cleophas, and scourged Peter and John; thus did the members partake of the sufferings of the Head, he was killed and crucified, and so were they. Christians must expect to resist unto blood. <div eID="gen23492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23493" type="x-p"/> 2. Their unwearied industry; <hi type="italic">Ye shall persecute them from city to city.</hi> As the apostles went from city to city, to preach the gospel, the Jews dodged them, and haunted them, and stirred up persecution against them, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.19">Acts xiv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.13">xvii. 13</reference>. They that <hi type="italic">did not believe in Judea</hi> were more bitter enemies to the gospel than any other unbelievers, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.31">Rom. xv. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen23493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23494" type="x-p"/> 3. The pretence of religion in this; they scourged them in their synagogues, their place of worship, where they kept their ecclesiastical courts; so that they did it as a piece of service to the church; cast them out, and said, <hi type="italic">Let the Lord be glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.2">John xvi. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen23494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23495" type="x-p"/> III. He imputes the sin of their fathers to them, because they imitated it; <hi type="italic">That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35-Matt.23.36">v. 35, 36</reference>. Though God bear long with a persecuting generation, he will not bear always; and patience abused, turns into the greatest wrath. The longer sinners have been heaping up treasures of wickedness, the deeper and fuller will the treasures of wrath be; and the breaking of them up will be like breaking up the fountains of the great deep. <div eID="gen23495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23496" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. The extent of this imputation; it takes in <hi type="italic">all the righteous blood shed upon the earth,</hi> that is, the blood shed for righteousness' sake, which has all been laid up in God's treasury, and not a drop of it lost, for <hi type="italic">it is precious.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Ps. lxxii. 14</reference>. He dates the account <hi type="italic">from the blood of righteous Abel,</hi> thence this <hi type="italic">æra martyrum—age of martyrs</hi>—commences; he is called <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> Abel, for he obtained witness from heaven, that he was <hi type="italic">righteous, God testifying of his gifts.</hi> How early did martyrdom come into the world! The first that died, died for his religion, and, <hi type="italic">being dead, he yet speaketh.</hi> His blood not only cried against Cain, but continues to cry against all that walk in the way of Cain, and hate and persecute their brother, <hi type="italic">because their works are righteous.</hi> He extends it <hi type="italic">to the blood of Zacharias, the son of Barachias</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.36">v. 36</reference>), not Zecharias the prophet (as some would have it), though he was <hi type="italic">the son of Barachias</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zech. i. 1.</reference>) nor Zecharias the father of John Baptist, as others say; but, as is most probable, <hi type="italic">Zechariah the son of Jehoiada,</hi> who was <hi type="italic">slain in the court of the Lord's house,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20-2Chr.24.21">2 Chron. xxiv. 20, 21</reference>. His father is called <hi type="italic">Barachias,</hi> which signifies much the same with Jehoiada; and it was usual among the Jews for the same person to have two names; <hi type="italic">whom ye slew,</hi> ye of this nation, though not of this generation. This is specified, because the requiring of that is particularly spoken of (<reference osisRef="2Chr.24.22">2 Chron. xxiv. 22</reference>), as that of Abel's is. The Jews imagined that the captivity had sufficiently atoned for the guilt; but Christ lets them know that it was not yet fully accounted for, but remained upon the score. And some think that this is mentioned with a prophetical hint, for there was one Zecharias, the son of Baruch, whom Josephus speaks of (<hi type="italic">War</hi> 4. 335), who was a just and good man, who was killed in the temple a little before it was destroyed by the Romans. Archbishop Tillotson thinks that Christ both alludes to the history of the former Zecharias in <hi type="italic">Chronicles,</hi> and foretels the death of this latter in Josephus. Though the latter was not yet slain, yet, before this destruction comes, it would be true that they had slain him; so that all shall be put together from first to last. <div eID="gen23496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23497" type="x-p"/> 2. The effect of it; <hi type="italic">All these things shall come;</hi> all the guilt of this blood, all the punishment of it, it shall <hi type="italic">all come upon this generation.</hi> The misery and ruin that are coming upon them, shall be so very great, that, though, considering the evil of their own sins, it was less that even those deserved; yet, comparing it with other judgments, it will seem to be a general reckoning for all the wickedness of their ancestors, especially their persecutions, to all which God declared this ruin to have special reference and relation. The destruction shall be so dreadful, as if God had once for all arraigned them for all the righteous blood shed in the world. It shall <hi type="italic">come upon this generation;</hi> which intimates, that it shall come quickly; some here shall live to see it. Note, The sorer and nearer the punishment of sin is, the louder is the call to repentance and reformation. <div eID="gen23497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23498" type="x-p"/> IV. He laments the wickedness of Jerusalem, and justly upbraids them with the many kind offers he had made them, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">v. 37</reference>. See with what concern he speaks of that city; <hi type="italic">O Jerusalem, Jerusalem!</hi> The repetition is emphatical, and bespeaks abundance of commiseration. A day or two before Christ had wept over Jerusalem, now he sighed and groaned over it. Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">the vision of peace</hi> (so it signifies), must now be the seat of war and confusion. Jerusalem, that had been <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth,</hi> must now be <hi type="italic">a hissing, and an astonishment, and a by-word;</hi> Jerusalem, that has been <hi type="italic">a city compact together,</hi> shall now be shattered and ruined by its own intestine broils. Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">the place that God has chosen to put his name there,</hi> shall now be abandoned to the spoil and the robbers, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1">Lam. i. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">iv. 1</reference>. But wherefore will the Lord do all this to Jerusalem? Why? <hi type="italic">Jerusalem hath grievously sinned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.1.8">Lam. i. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen23498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23499" type="x-p"/> 1. She persecuted God's messengers; <hi type="italic">Thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee.</hi> This sin is especially charged upon Jerusalem; because there the Sanhedrim, or great council, sat, who took cognizance of church matters, and therefore a prophet could not perish but in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.33">Luke xiii. 33</reference>. It is true, they had not now a power to put any man to death, but they killed the prophets in popular tumults, mobbed them, as Stephen, and put the Roman powers on to kill them. At Jerusalem, where the gospel was first preached, it was first persecuted (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.1">Acts viii. 1</reference>), and that place was the head-quarters of the persecutors; thence warrants were issued out to other cities, and thither the saints were brought bound, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.2">Acts ix. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou stonest them:</hi> that was a capital punishment, in use only among the Jews. By the law, false prophets and seducers were to <hi type="italic">be stoned</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.10">Deut. xiii. 10</reference>), under colour of which law, they put the true prophets to death. Note, It has often been the artifice of Satan, to turn that artillery against the church, which was originally planted in the defence of it. Brand the true prophets as seducers, and the true professors of religion as heretics and schismatics, and then it will be easy to persecute them. There was abundance of other wickedness in Jerusalem; but this was the sin that made the loudest cry, and which God had an eye to more than any other, in bringing that ruin upon them, as <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.16">2 Chron. xxxvi. 16</reference>. Observe, Christ speaks in the present tense; <hi type="italic">Thou killest, and stonest;</hi> for all they had done, and all they would do, was present to Christ's notice. <div eID="gen23499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23500" type="x-p"/> 2. She refused and rejected Christ, and gospel offers. The former was a sin <hi type="italic">without</hi> remedy, this <hi type="italic">against</hi> the remedy. Here is, (1.) The wonderful grace and favour of Jesus Christ toward them; <hi type="italic">How often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen gathers her chickens under her wings!</hi> Thus kind and condescending are the offers of gospel grace, even to Jerusalem's children, bad as she is, the inhabitants, the little ones not excepted. [1.] The favour proposed was the gathering of them. Christ's design is to gather poor souls, gather them in from their wanderings, gather them home to himself, as the Centre of unity; for <hi type="italic">to him must the gathering of the people be.</hi> He would have taken the whole body of the Jewish nation into the church, and so gathered them all (as the Jews used to speak of proselytes) <hi type="italic">under the wings of the Divine Majesty.</hi> It is here illustrated by a humble similitude; <hi type="italic">as a hen</hi> clucks <hi type="italic">her chickens together.</hi> Christ would have gathered them, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> With such a tenderness of affection as the hen does, which has, by instinct, a peculiar concern for her young ones. Christ's gathering of souls, comes from his love, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer. xxxi. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> For the same end. <hi type="italic">The hen gathered her chickens under her wings,</hi> for protection and safety, and for warmth and comfort; poor souls have in Christ both refuge and refreshment. The chickens naturally run to the hen for shelter, when they are threatened by the birds of prey; perhaps Christ refers to that promise (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Ps. xci. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">He shall cover thee with his feathers.</hi> There is <hi type="italic">healing under Christ's wings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.2">Mal. iv. 2</reference>); that is more than the hen has for her chickens. <div eID="gen23500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23501" type="x-p"/> [2.] The forwardness of Christ to confer this favour. His offers are, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Very free; <hi type="italic">I would have done it.</hi> Jesus Christ is truly willing to receive and save poor souls that come to him. He desires not their ruin, he delights in their repentance. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Very frequent; <hi type="italic">How often!</hi> Christ often came up to Jerusalem, preached, and wrought miracles there; and the meaning of all this, was, he would have gathered them. He keeps account how often his calls have been repeated. As often as we have heard the sound of the gospel, as often as we have felt the strivings of the Spirit, so often Christ would have gathered us. <div eID="gen23501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23502" type="x-p"/> [3.] Their wilful refusal of this grace and favour; <hi type="italic">Ye would not.</hi> How emphatically is their obstinacy opposed to Christ's mercy! I would, and <hi type="italic">ye would not.</hi> He was willing to save them, but they were not willing to be saved by him. Note, It is wholly owing to the wicked wills of sinners, that they are not gathered under the wings of the Lord Jesus. They did not like the terms upon which Christ proposed to gather them; they loved their sins, and yet trusted to their righteousness; they would not submit either to the grace of Christ or to his government, and so the bargain broke off. <div eID="gen23502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23503" type="x-p"/> V. He reads Jerusalem's doom (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.38-Matt.23.39">v. 38, 39</reference>); <hi type="italic">Therefore behold your house is left unto you desolate.</hi> Both the city and the temple, God's house and their own, all shall be laid waste. But it is especially meant of the temple, which they boasted of, and trusted to; that holy mountain because of which they were so haughty. Note, they that will not be gathered by the love and grace of Christ shall be consumed and scattered by his wrath; <hi type="italic">I would, and you would not. Israel would none of me, so I gave them up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.81.11-Ps.81.12">Ps. lxxxi. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen23503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23504" type="x-p"/> 1. Their house shall be <hi type="italic">deserted; It is left unto you.</hi> Christ was now departing from the temple, and never came into it again, but by this word abandoned it to ruin. They doated on it, would have it to themselves; Christ must have no room or interest there. "Well," saith Christ, "it is left to you; take it, and make your best of it; I will never have any thing more to do with it." They had made it <hi type="italic">a house of merchandise, and a den of thieves,</hi> and so it is left to them. Not long after this, the voice was heard in the temple, "Let us depart hence." When Christ went, <hi type="italic">Ichabod, the glory departed.</hi> Their city also was left to them, destitute of God's presence and grace; he was no longer <hi type="italic">a wall of fire about them,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">the glory in the midst of them.</hi> <div eID="gen23504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23505" type="x-p"/> 2. It shall be <hi type="italic">desolate; It is left unto you desolate;</hi> it is left <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eremos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">a wilderness.</hi> (1.) It was immediately, when Christ left it, in the eyes of all that understood themselves, a very dismal melancholy place. Christ's departure makes the best furnished, best replenished place a wilderness, though it be the temple, the chief place of concourse; for what comfort can there be where Christ is not? Though there may be a crowd of other contentments, yet, if Christ's special spiritual presence be withdrawn, that soul, that place, is <hi type="italic">become a wilderness, a land of darkness, as darkness itself.</hi> This comes of men's rejecting Christ, and driving him away from them. (2.) It was, not long after, destroyed and ruined, and <hi type="italic">not one stone left upon another.</hi> The lot of Jerusalem's enemies will now become Jerusalem's lot, <hi type="italic">to be made of a city a heap, of a defenced city a ruin</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa. xxv. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">a lofty city laid low, even to the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5">Isa. xxvi. 5</reference>. The temple, that holy and beautiful house, became desolate. When God goes out, all enemies break in. <div eID="gen23505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23506" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is the final farewell that Christ took of them and their temple; <hi type="italic">Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh.</hi> This bespeaks, <div eID="gen23506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23507" type="x-p"/> 1. His departure from them. The time was at hand, when <hi type="italic">he should leave the world, to go to his Father,</hi> and be seen no more. <hi type="italic">After his resurrection, he was seen only by a few chosen witnesses,</hi> and they saw him not long, but he soon removed to the invisible world, and there will be <hi type="italic">till the time of the restitution of all things,</hi> when his welcome at his first coming will be repeated with loud acclamations; <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.</hi> Christ will not be seen again till he <hi type="italic">come in the clouds, and every eye shall see him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.7">Rev. i. 7</reference>); and then, even they, who, when time was, rejected and pierced him, will be glad to come in among his adorers; then every knee shall bow to him, even those that had bowed to Baal; and even the workers of iniquity will then cry, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord,</hi> and will own, when his wrath is kindled, that <hi type="italic">blessed are all they that put their trust in him.</hi> Would we have our lot in that day with those that say, <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that cometh?</hi> let us be with them now, with them that truly worship, and truly welcome, Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen23507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23508" type="x-p"/> 2. Their continued blindness and obstinacy; <hi type="italic">Ye shall not see me,</hi> that is, not see me to be the Messiah (for otherwise they did see him upon the cross), not see the light of the truth concerning me, nor <hi type="italic">the things that belong to your peace, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh.</hi> They will never be convinced, till Christ's second coming convince them, when it will be too late to make an interest in him, and nothing will remain <hi type="italic">but a fearful looking for of judgment.</hi> Note, (1.) Wilful blindness is often punished with judicial blindness. If they <hi type="italic">will</hi> not see, they <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not see. With this word he concludes his public preaching. <hi type="italic">After his resurrection,</hi> which was <hi type="italic">the sign of the prophet Jonas,</hi> they should have no other sign given them, till they should <hi type="italic">see the sign of the Son of man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.30">ch. xxiv. 30</reference>. (2.) When <hi type="italic">the Lord comes with ten thousand of his saints,</hi> he will convince all, and will force acknowledgments from the proudest of his enemies, of his being the Messiah, and even <hi type="italic">they shall be found liars to him.</hi> They that would not now come at his call, shall then be forced to depart with his curse. The chief priests and scribes were displeased with the children for crying <hi type="italic">hosanna</hi> to Christ; but the day is coming, when proud persecutors would gladly be found in the condition of the meanest and poorest they now trample upon. They who now reproach and ridicule the hosannas of the saints will be of another mind shortly; it were therefore better to be of that mind now. Some make this to refer to the conversion of the Jews to the faith of Christ; then they shall see him, and own him, and <hi type="italic">say, Blessed is he that cometh;</hi> but it seems rather to look further, for the complete manifestation of Christ, and conviction of sinners, are reserved to be the glory of the last day.  <chapter eID="Matt.23"/> <div eID="gen23508" type="x-p"/>

entries.f836069bc567d80bead99f9dd0bcb8b762dea75f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13756"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.39">Mt 23:1-39</reference>. Denunciation of the Scribes and Pharisees--Lamentation over Jerusalem, and Farewell to the Temple. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.12.38-Mark.12.40">Mr 12:38-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.45-Luke.20.47">Lu 20:45-47</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26395" type="x-p"/> For this long and terrible discourse we are indebted, with the exception of a few verses in Mark and Luke, to Matthew alone. But as it is only an extended repetition of denunciations uttered not long before at the table of a Pharisee, and recorded by Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.37-Luke.11.54">Lu 11:37-54</reference>), we may take both together in the exposition.<div eID="gen26395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26396" type="x-p"/> Denunciation of the Scribes and Pharisees (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.1-Matt.23.36">Mt 23:1-36</reference>).<div eID="gen26396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26397" type="x-p"/> The first twelve verses were addressed more immediately to the disciples, the rest to the scribes and Pharisees.<div eID="gen26397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13756"/><hi type="bold">1. Then spake Jesus to the multitude--</hi>to the multitudes, "and to his disciples." <div eID="gen26398" type="x-p"/>
entries.78e062ff5925e04c1073cd123218523983786446: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13757"/><div sID="gen26399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13757"/><hi type="bold">2. Saying, The scribes and the Pharisees sit--</hi>The Jewish teachers stood to read, but sat to expound the Scriptures, as will be seen by comparing <reference osisRef="Luke.4.16">Lu 4:16</reference> with <reference osisRef="Luke.4.20">Lu 4:20</reference>.<div eID="gen26399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Moses' seat--</hi>that is, as interpreters of the law given by Moses. <div eID="gen26400" type="x-p"/>
entries.fca94ca5c7d94155b24beac50e94af166bf2039f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13758"/><div sID="gen26401" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13758"/><hi type="bold">3. All therefore--</hi>that is, all which, as sitting in that seat and teaching out of that law.<div eID="gen26401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they bid you observe, that observe and do--</hi>The word "therefore" is thus, it will be seen, of great importance, as limiting those injunctions which He would have them obey to what they fetched from the law itself. In requiring implicit obedience to such injunctions, He would have them to recognize the authority with which they taught over and above the obligations of the law itself--an important principle truly; but He who denounced the traditions of such teachers (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.3">Mt 15:3</reference>) cannot have meant here to throw His shield over these. It is remarked by Webster and Wilkinson that the warning to beware of the scribes is given by Mark and Luke (<reference osisRef="Mark.12.38">Mr 12:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.20.46">Lu 20:46</reference>) without any qualification: the charge to respect and obey them being reported by Matthew alone, indicating for whom this Gospel was especially written, and the writer's desire to conciliate the Jews. <div eID="gen26402" type="x-p"/>
entries.8452c0073d2c849c378051641e1b831daf43e238: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13759"/><div sID="gen26403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13759"/><hi type="bold">4. For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them--</hi>"touch them not" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.46">Lu 11:46</reference>).<div eID="gen26403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with one of their fingers--</hi>referring not so much to the irksomeness of the legal rites, though they were irksome enough (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">Ac 15:10</reference>), as to the heartless rigor with which they were enforced, and by men of shameless inconsistency. <div eID="gen26404" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c4dac321aaeaed9550d245f154ecb676c45f521: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13760"/><div sID="gen26405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13760"/><hi type="bold">5. But all their works they do for to be seen of men--</hi>Whatever good they do, or zeal they show, has but one motive--human applause.<div eID="gen26405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they make broad their phylacteries--</hi>strips of parchment with Scripture-texts on them, worn on the forehead, arm, and side, in time of prayer.<div eID="gen26406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and enlarge the borders of their garments--</hi>fringes of their upper garments (<reference osisRef="Num.15.37-Num.15.40">Nu 15:37-40</reference>). <div eID="gen26407" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad4f24e021cd1b7436a9dbe2f771816db7ba8ea1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13761"/><div sID="gen26408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13761"/><hi type="bold">6. And love the uppermost rooms at feasts--</hi>The word "room" is now obsolete in the sense here intended. It should be "the uppermost place," that is, the place of highest honor.<div eID="gen26408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26409" type="x-p"/> and the chief seats in the synagogues. See on <reference osisRef="Luke.14.7">Lu 14:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen26409" type="x-p"/>
entries.c83c0125de05d5f378f334ef8ceae089504ae34f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13762"/><div sID="gen26410" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13762"/><hi type="bold">7. And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi--</hi>It is the spirit rather than the letter of this that must be pressed; though the violation of the letter, springing from spiritual pride, has done incalculable evil in the Church of Christ. The reiteration of the word "Rabbi" shows how it tickled the ear and fed the spiritual pride of those ecclesiastics. <div eID="gen26410" type="x-p"/>
entries.903cd41cb77916ab263c8bd95128aebc9ebd1723: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13763"/><div sID="gen26411" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13763"/><hi type="bold">8. But be not ye called Rabbi; for one is your Master--</hi>your Guide, your Teacher. <div eID="gen26411" type="x-p"/>
entries.329a7415a63460f6c31cfc5b9489f00ba9e11d40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13764"/><div sID="gen26412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13764"/><hi type="bold">9. And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven, &c.--</hi>To construe these injunctions into a condemnation of every title by which Church rulers may be distinguished from the flock which they rule, is virtually to condemn that rule itself; and accordingly the same persons do both--but against the whole strain of the New Testament and sound Christian judgment. But when we have guarded ourselves against these extremes, let us see to it that we retain the full spirit of this warning against that itch for ecclesiastical superiority which has been the bane and the scandal of Christ's ministers in every age. (On the use of the word "Christ" here, see on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.1">Mt 1:1</reference>). <div eID="gen26412" type="x-p"/>
entries.464edb5575b610061f6b045b376e244d9644f906: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13765"/><div sID="gen26413" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13765"/><hi type="bold">11. But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant--</hi>This plainly means, "shall show that he is so by becoming your servant"; as in <reference osisRef="Matt.20.27">Mt 20:27</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Mark.10.44">Mr 10:44</reference>. <div eID="gen26413" type="x-p"/>
entries.54b82f9c96cbc069f7cdc564916ce246660346ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13766"/><div sID="gen26414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13766"/><hi type="bold">12. And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Luke.18.14">Lu 18:14</reference>. What follows was addressed more immediately to the scribes and Pharisees. <div eID="gen26414" type="x-p"/>
entries.d45ee92561035c524223839abdf2f35664ad1461: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13767"/><div sID="gen26415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13767"/><hi type="bold">13. But woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men--</hi>Here they are charged with shutting heaven against men: in <reference osisRef="Luke.11.52">Lu 11:52</reference> they are charged with what was worse, taking away the key--"the key of knowledge"--which means, not the key to open knowledge, but knowledge as the only key to open heaven. A right knowledge of God's revealed word is eternal life, as our Lord says (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.39">5:39</reference>); but this they took away from the people, substituting for it their wretched traditions. <div eID="gen26415" type="x-p"/>
entries.c43a369e23f752d0f0ae4f894c2ea6ec6f38f15c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13768"/><div sID="gen26416" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13768"/><hi type="bold">14. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows' houses, &c.--</hi>Taking advantage of the helpless condition and confiding character of "widows," they contrived to obtain possession of their property, while by their "long prayers" they made them believe they were raised far above "filthy lucre." So much "the greater damnation" awaits them. What a lifelike description of the Romish clergy, the true successors of those scribes! <div eID="gen26416" type="x-p"/>
entries.4aa1101570662750b477f7de7996b436372840d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13769"/><div sID="gen26417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13769"/><hi type="bold">15. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte--</hi>from heathenism. We have evidence of this in Josephus.<div eID="gen26417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves--</hi>condemned, for the hypocrisy he would learn to practice, both by the religion he left and that he embraced. <div eID="gen26418" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac9e28a336037f7b41593f4d2f9d031390a81857: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13770"/><div sID="gen26419" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13770"/><hi type="bold">16. Woe unto you, ye blind guides--</hi>Striking expression this of the ruinous effects of erroneous teaching. Our Lord, here and in some following verses, condemns the subtle distinctions they made as to the sanctity of oaths--distinctions invented only to promote their own avaricious purposes.<div eID="gen26419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing--</hi>He has incurred no debt.<div eID="gen26420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple--</hi>meaning not the gold that adorned the temple itself, but the Corban, set apart for sacred uses (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.15.5">Mt 15:5</reference>).<div eID="gen26421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is a debtor!--</hi>that is, it is no longer his own, even though the necessities of the parent might require it. We know who the successors of these men are.<div eID="gen26422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but whosoever sweareth by the gift that is upon it, he is guilty--</hi>It should have been rendered, "he is a debtor," as in <reference osisRef="Matt.23.16">Mt 23:16</reference>. <div eID="gen26423" type="x-p"/>
entries.040663fc9a9c0e0b55c90b4fb44fc422cc9b3aed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13771"/><div sID="gen26424" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13771"/><hi type="bold">19. Ye fools, and blind! for whether is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifieth the gift?--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Exod.29.37">Ex 29:37</reference>). <div eID="gen26424" type="x-p"/>
entries.ad5ade12b9b925021071cec3f1c94455bf409ba3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13772"/><div sID="gen26425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13772"/><hi type="bold">20-22. Whoso therefore shall swear by the altar, &c.--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.5.33-Matt.5.37">Mt 5:33-37</reference>. <div eID="gen26425" type="x-p"/>
entries.394b0a46e51704de901de68f34883408e61cb4e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13773"/><div sID="gen26426" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13773"/><hi type="bold">23. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise--</hi>rather, "dill," as in Margin.<div eID="gen26426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and cummin--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.42">Lu 11:42</reference>) it is "and rue, and all manner of herbs." They grounded this practice on <reference osisRef="Lev.27.30">Le 27:30</reference>, which they interpreted rigidly. Our Lord purposely names the most trifling products of the earth as examples of what they punctiliously exacted the tenth of.<div eID="gen26427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26428" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.42">Lu 11:42</reference>) it is "judgment, mercy, and the love of God"--the expression being probably varied by our Lord Himself on the two different occasions. In both His reference is to <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mi 6:6-8</reference>, where the prophet makes all acceptable religion to consist of three elements--"doing justly, loving mercy, and walking humbly with our God"; which third element presupposes and comprehends both the "faith" of Matthew and the "love" of Luke. See on <reference osisRef="Mark.12.29">Mr 12:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.12.32">Mr 12:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.12.33">33</reference>. The same tendency to merge greater duties in less besets even the children of God; but it is the characteristic of hypocrites.<div eID="gen26428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26429" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone--</hi>There is no need for one set of duties to jostle out another; but it is to be carefully noted that of the greater duties our Lord says, "Ye ought to have done" them, while of the lesser He merely says, "Ye ought not to leave them undone." <div eID="gen26429" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c2c0bfc9b2fb009289a22a7f79e22423692bb64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13774"/><div sID="gen26430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13774"/><hi type="bold">24. Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat--</hi>The proper rendering--as in the older English translations, and perhaps our own as it came from the translators' hands--evidently is, "strain out." It was the custom, says Trench, of the stricter Jews to strain their wine, vinegar, and other potables through linen or gauze, lest unawares they should drink down some little unclean insect therein and thus transgress (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.20">Le 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.41">23, 41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.42">42</reference>)--just as the Buddhists do now in Ceylon and Hindustan--and to this custom of theirs our Lord here refers.<div eID="gen26430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and swallow a camel--</hi>the largest animal the Jews knew, as the "gnat" was the smallest; both were by the law unclean. <div eID="gen26431" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a50605599755cfb7473dca5302c9729a711554d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13775"/><div sID="gen26432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13775"/><hi type="bold">25. within they are full of extortion--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.39">Lu 11:39</reference>) the same word is rendered "ravening," that is, "rapacity." <div eID="gen26432" type="x-p"/>
entries.32f92a83c752b993cc62172c8c248410e8c76664: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13776"/><div sID="gen26433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13776"/><hi type="bold">26. Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.40">Lu 11:40</reference>) it is, "Ye fools, did not He that made that which is without make that which is within also?"--"He to whom belongs the outer life, and of right demands its subjection to Himself, is the inner man less His?" A remarkable example this of our Lord's power of drawing the most striking illustrations of great truths from the most familiar objects and incidents in life. To these words, recorded by Luke, He adds the following, involving a principle of immense value: "But rather give alms of such things as ye have, and behold, all things are clean unto you" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.41">Lu 11:41</reference>). As the greed of these hypocrites was one of the most prominent features of their character (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.14">Lu 16:14</reference>), our Lord bids them exemplify the opposite character, and then their outside, ruled by this, would be beautiful in the eye of God, and their meals would be eaten with clean hands, though much fouled with the business of this everyday world. (See <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7">Ec 9:7</reference>). <div eID="gen26433" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e483ea7ef770692a28aaa6c6d63e034d61ab631: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13777"/><div sID="gen26434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13777"/><hi type="bold">27. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like whited sepulchres--</hi>or, whitewashed sepulchres. (Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.23.3">Ac 23:3</reference>). The process of whitewashing the sepulchres, as Lightfoot says, was performed on a certain day every year, not for ceremonial cleansing, but, as the following words seem rather to imply, to beautify them.<div eID="gen26434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26435" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness--</hi>What a powerful way of conveying the charge, that with all their fair show their hearts were full of corruption! (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">Psa 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13">Ro 3:13</reference>). But our Lord, stripping off the figure, next holds up their iniquity in naked colors.<div eID="gen26435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets--</hi>that is, "ye be witnesses that ye have inherited, and voluntarily served yourselves heirs to, the truth-hating, prophet-killing, spirit of your fathers." Out of pretended respect and honor, they repaired and beautified the sepulchres of the prophets, and with whining hypocrisy said, "If we had been in their days, how differently should we have treated these prophets?" While all the time they were witnesses to themselves that they were the children of them that killed the prophets, convicting themselves daily of as exact a resemblance in spirit and character to the very classes over whose deeds they pretended to mourn, as child to parent. In <reference osisRef="Luke.11.44">Lu 11:44</reference> our Lord gives another turn to this figure of a grave: "Ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them." As one might unconsciously walk over a grave concealed from view, and thus contract ceremonial defilement, so the plausible exterior of the Pharisees kept people from perceiving the pollution they contracted from coming in contact with such corrupt characters. <div eID="gen26436" type="x-p"/>
entries.12f6a38cb4243741a0a77aac99a014fbce418001: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13778"/><div sID="gen26437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13778"/><hi type="bold">33. Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?--</hi>In thus, at the end of His ministry, recalling the words of the Baptist at the outset of his, our Lord would seem to intimate that the only difference between their condemnation now and then was, that now they were ripe for their doom, which they were not then. <div eID="gen26437" type="x-p"/>
entries.868926f37b5de57ad3f92a9ead88713866bc917a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13779"/><div sID="gen26438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13779"/><hi type="bold">34. Wherefore, behold, I send unto you prophets, and wise men, and scribes--</hi>The I here is emphatic: "I am sending," that is, "am about to send." In <reference osisRef="Luke.11.49">Lu 11:49</reference> the variation is remarkable: "Therefore also, said the wisdom of God, I will send them," &c. What precisely is meant by "the wisdom of God" here, is somewhat difficult to determine. To us it appears to be simply an announcement of a purpose of the Divine Wisdom, in the high style of ancient prophecy, to send a last set of messengers whom the people would reject, and rejecting, would fill up the cup of their iniquity. But, whereas in Luke it is "I, the Wisdom of God, will send them," in Matthew it is "I, Jesus, am sending them"; language only befitting the one sender of all the prophets, the Lord God of Israel now in the flesh. They are evidently evangelical messengers, but called by the familiar Jewish names of "prophets, wise men, and scribes," whose counterparts were the inspired and gifted servants of the Lord Jesus; for in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.49">Lu 11:49</reference>) it is "prophets and apostles."<div eID="gen26438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar--</hi>As there is no record of any fresh murder answering to this description, probably the allusion is not to any recent murder, but to <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20-2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:20-22</reference>, as the last recorded and most suitable case for illustration. And as Zacharias' last words were, "The Lord require it," so they are here warned that of that generation it should be required. <div eID="gen26439" type="x-p"/>
entries.747c8ccc0767dfd73475f7781a1ec535b3c8330d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13780"/><div sID="gen26440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13780"/><hi type="bold">36. Verily I say unto you, All these things shall come upon this generation--</hi>As it was only in the last generation of them that "the iniquity of the Amorites was full" (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Ge 15:16</reference>), and then the abominations of ages were at once completely and awfully avenged, so the iniquity of Israel was allowed to accumulate from age to age till in that generation it came to the full, and the whole collected vengeance of heaven broke at once over its devoted head. In the first French Revolution the same awful principle was exemplified, and Christendom has not done with it yet.<div eID="gen26440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26441" type="x-p"/> Lamentation over Jerusalem, and Farewell to the Temple (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37-Matt.23.39">Mt 23:37-39</reference>). <div eID="gen26441" type="x-p"/>
entries.908c40c009d7f023f2888b8e8a23d6565fa8fa15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13781"/><div sID="gen26442" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13781"/><hi type="bold">37. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, &c.--</hi>How ineffably grand and melting is this apostrophe! It is the very heart of God pouring itself forth through human flesh and speech. It is this incarnation of the innermost life and love of Deity, pleading with men, bleeding for them, and ascending only to open His arms to them and win them back by the power of this story of matchless love, that has conquered the world, that will yet "draw all men unto Him," and beautify and ennoble Humanity itself! "Jerusalem" here does not mean the mere city or its inhabitants; nor is it to be viewed merely as the metropolis of the nation, but as the center of their religious life--"the city of their solemnities, whither the tribes went up, to give thanks unto the name of the Lord"; and at this moment it was full of them. It is the whole family of God, then, which is here apostrophized by a name dear to every Jew, recalling to him all that was distinctive and precious in his religion. The intense feeling that sought vent in this utterance comes out first in the redoubling of the opening word--"Jerusalem, Jerusalem!" but, next, in the picture of it which He draws--"that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee!"--not content with spurning God's messages of mercy, that canst not suffer even the messengers to live! When He adds, "How often would I have gathered thee!" He refers surely to something beyond the six or seven times that He visited and taught in Jerusalem while on earth. No doubt it points to "the prophets," whom they "killed," to "them that were sent unto her," whom they "stoned." But whom would He have gathered so often? "Thee," truth-hating, mercy-spurning, prophet-killing Jerusalem--how often would I have gathered thee! Compare with this that affecting clause in the great ministerial commission, "that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in His name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem!" (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Lu 24:47</reference>). What encouragement to the heartbroken at their own long-continued and obstinate rebellion! But we have not yet got at the whole heart of this outburst. I would have gathered thee, He says, "even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings." Was ever imagery so homely invested with such grace and such sublimity as this, at our Lord's touch? And yet how exquisite the figure itself--of protection, rest, warmth, and all manner of conscious well-being in those poor, defenseless, dependent little creatures, as they creep under and feel themselves overshadowed by the capacious and kindly wing of the mother bird! If, wandering beyond hearing of her peculiar call, they are overtaken by a storm or attacked by an enemy, what can they do but in the one case droop and die, and in the other submit to be torn in pieces? But if they can reach in time their place of safety, under the mother's wing, in vain will any enemy try to drag them thence. For rising into strength, kindling into fury, and forgetting herself entirely in her young, she will let the last drop of her blood be shed out and perish in defense of her precious charge, rather than yield them to an enemy's talons. How significant all this of what Jesus is and does for men! Under His great Mediatorial wing would He have "gathered" Israel. For the figure, see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.10-Deut.32.12">De 32:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.12">Ru 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.7">36:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">61:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.7">63:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">91:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">Is 31:5</reference>; Mal 4:2. The ancient rabbins had a beautiful expression for proselytes from the heathen--that they had "come under the wings of the Shekinah." For this last word, see on <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Mt 23:38</reference>. But what was the result of all this tender and mighty love? The answer is, "And ye would not." O mysterious word! <hi type="bold">mysterious the resistance of such patient Love--</hi>mysterious the liberty of self-undoing! The awful dignity of the will, as here expressed, might make the ears to tingle. <div eID="gen26442" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b31fa31175001913b69cd938ac4a434e0bf2fdb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13782"/><div sID="gen26443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13782"/><hi type="bold">38. Behold, your house--</hi>the temple, beyond all doubt; but their house now, not the Lord's. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.22.7">Mt 22:7</reference>.<div eID="gen26443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26444" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is left unto you desolate--</hi>deserted, that is, of its Divine Inhabitant. But who is that? Hear the next words: <div eID="gen26444" type="x-p"/>
entries.e23c18246145730c16da0eb1a5a72ca5c1b5c7f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13783"/><div sID="gen26445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13783"/><hi type="bold">39. For I say unto you--</hi>and these were His last words to the impenitent nation, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.13.1">Mr 13:1</reference>, opening remarks.<div eID="gen26445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26446" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ye shall not see me henceforth--</hi>What? Does Jesus mean that He was Himself the Lord of the temple, and that it became "deserted" when He finally left it? It is even so. Now is thy fate sealed, O Jerusalem, for the glory is departed from thee! That glory, once visible in the holy of holies, over the mercy seat, when on the day of atonement the blood of typical expiation was sprinkled on it and in front of it--called by the Jews the Shekinah, or the Dwelling, as being the visible pavilion of Jehovah--that glory, which Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.13">Is 6:1-13</reference>) saw in vision, the beloved disciple says was the glory of Christ (<reference osisRef="John.12.41">Joh 12:41</reference>). Though it was never visible in the second temple, Haggai foretold that "the glory of that latter house should be greater than of the former" (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>) because "the Lord whom they sought was suddenly to come to His temple" (Mal 3:1), not in a mere bright cloud, but enshrined in living humanity! Yet brief as well as "sudden" was the manifestation to be: for the words He was now uttering were to be His very last within its precincts.<div eID="gen26446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord--</hi>that is, till those "Hosannas to the Son of David" with which the multitude had welcomed Him into the city--instead of "sore displeasing the chief priests and scribes" (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.15">Mt 21:15</reference>)--should break forth from the whole nation, as their glad acclaim to their once pierced, but now acknowledged, Messiah. That such a time will come is clear from <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">2Co 3:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.16">16</reference>, &c. In what sense they shall then "see Him" may be gathered from <reference osisRef="Zech.2.10-Zech.2.13">Zec 2:10-13</reference>; Eze 37:23-28; 39:28, 29, &c. <chapter eID="Matt.23"/>

entries.82f2d092702d5e7b22abc094cb922823648f38bd: <div eID="gen38243" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen38244" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38245" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38245" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen38244" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen38246" type="x-p"/> The character of the scribes and Pharisees, and directions to the people and the disciples to receive the law from them, but not to follow their bad example, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.1-Mat.23.7">Mat 23:1-7</reference>. The disciples exhorted to humility, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.8-Mat.23.12">Mat 23:8-12</reference>. Different woes pronounced against the scribes and Pharisees for their intolerance, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.13">Mat 23:13</reference>; rapacity, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.14">Mat 23:14</reference>; false zeal, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.15">Mat 23:15</reference>; superstition in oaths and tithes, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.16-Mat.23.23">Mat 23:16-23</reference>; hypocrisy, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.24-Mat.23.28">Mat 23:24-28</reference>. Their cruelty, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.29-Mat.23.32">Mat 23:29-32</reference>. Their persecution of the apostles, etc. Their destruction foretold, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.33-Mat.23.36">Mat 23:33-36</reference>. Christ's lamentation over Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.37-Mat.23.39">Mat 23:37-39</reference>.
entries.07a5f06672a0fe1500b24ce4ac4671a3eb1cde7f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen38246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38247" type="x-p"/> The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat - Εκαθισαν. - They sat there formerly by Divine appointment: they sit there now by Divine permission. What our Lord says here refers to their expounding the Scriptures, for it was the custom of the Jewish doctors to sit while they expounded the law and prophets, (<reference osisRef="Mat.5.1">Mat 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.4.20-Luk.4.22">Luk 4:20-22</reference>), and to stand up when they read them. <div eID="gen38247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38248" type="x-p"/> By the seat of Moses, we are to understand authority to teach the law. Moses was the great teacher of the Jewish people; and the scribes, etc., are here represented as his successors.
entries.790323700b930e528374fa561871c0d0bc94d0e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen38248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38249" type="x-p"/> All therefore whatsoever - That is, all those things which they read out of the law and prophets, and all things which they teach consistently with them. This must be our Lord's meaning: he could not have desired them to do every thing, without restriction, which the Jewish doctors taught; because himself warns his disciples against their false teaching, and testifies that they had made the word of God of none effect by their traditions. See <reference osisRef="Mat.15.6">Mat 15:6</reference>, etc. Besides, as our Lord speaks here in the past tense - whatsoever they Have commanded, ὁσα ειπωσιν, he may refer to the teaching of a former period, when they taught the way of God in truth, or were much less corrupted than they were now.
entries.199903b31f75569bebd49ec412657ac443b8189d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen38249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38250" type="x-p"/> They bind heavy burdens - They are now so corrupt that they have added to the ceremonies of the law others of their own invention, which are not only burdensome and oppressive, but have neither reason, expediency, nor revelation, to countenance them. In a word, like all their successors in spirit to the present day, they were severe to others, but very indulgent to themselves.
entries.3924715eeb48f195c845619a367c39dfa9eb80b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen38250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38251" type="x-p"/> All their works they do for to be seen of men - In pointing out the corruptions of these men, our Lord gives us the distinguishing characteristics of all false teachers, whether Jewish or Christian. <div eID="gen38251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38252" type="x-p"/> 1. They live not according to the truths they preach. They say, and do not, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.3">Mat 23:3</reference>. <div eID="gen38252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38253" type="x-p"/> 2. They are severe to others, point out the narrowest road to heaven, and walk in the broad road themselves. They bind on burdens, etc., <reference osisRef="Mat.23.4">Mat 23:4</reference>. <div eID="gen38253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38254" type="x-p"/> 3. They affect to appear righteous, and are strict observers of certain rites, etc., while destitute of the power of godliness. They make broad their phylacteries, etc., <reference osisRef="Mat.23.5">Mat 23:5</reference>. <div eID="gen38254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38255" type="x-p"/> 4. They love worldly entertainments, go to feast wherever they are asked, and seek Church preferments. They love the chief places at feasts, and chief seats in the synagogues, <reference osisRef="Mat.23.6">Mat 23:6</reference>. <div eID="gen38255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38256" type="x-p"/> 5. They love and seek public respect and high titles, salutations in the market-place, (for they are seldom in their studies), and to be called of men rabbi - eminent teacher, though they have no title to it, either from the excellence or fruit of their teaching. When these marks are found in a man who professes to be a minister of Christ, charity itself will assert he is a thief and a robber - he has climbed over the wall of the sheepfold, or broken it down in order to get in. <div eID="gen38256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38257" type="x-p"/> Phylacteries - φυλακτηρια, from φυλασσω, to keep or preserve. These were small slips of parchment or vellum, on which certain portions of the law were written. The Jews tied these about their foreheads and arms, for three different purposes. <div eID="gen38257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38258" type="x-p"/> 1. To put them in mind of those precepts which they should constantly observe. <div eID="gen38258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38259" type="x-p"/> 2. To procure them reverence and respect in the sight of the heathen. And <div eID="gen38259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38260" type="x-p"/> 3. To act as amulets or charms to drive away evil spirits. <div eID="gen38260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38261" type="x-p"/> The first use of these phylacteries is evident from their name. <div eID="gen38261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38262" type="x-p"/> The second use appears from what is said on the subject from the Gemara, Beracoth, chap. 1., quoted by Kypke. "Whence is it proved that phylacteries, (תפילין, tephilin), are the strength of Israel? - Ans. From what is written, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.10">Deu 28:10</reference>. All the, people of the earth shall see that thou art called by the name [of יהוה Jehovah] - and they shall be afraid of thee. <div eID="gen38262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38263" type="x-p"/> The third use of them appears from the Targum, on <reference osisRef="Sol.8.3">Sol 8:3</reference> : His left hand is under my head, etc. "The congregation of Israel hath said, I am elect above all people, because I bind my phylacteries on my left hand, and on my head, and the scroll is fixed to the right side of my gate, the third part of which looks to my bed-chamber, that Daemons may not be permitted to Injure me." <div eID="gen38263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38264" type="x-p"/> An original phylactery lies now before me. It is a piece of fine vellum, about eighteen inches long, and an inch and quarter broad. It is divided into four unequal compartments: in the first is written, in a very fair character, with many apices, after the mode of the German Jews, the first ten verses of Exod. 13; in the second compartment is written, from the eleventh to the sixteenth verse of the same chapter, inclusive in the third, from the fourth to the ninth verse, inclusive, of Deut. 6., beginning with, Hear, O Israel, etc.; in the fourth, from the thirteenth to the twenty-first verse, inclusive, of Deut. 11. <div eID="gen38264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38265" type="x-p"/> These passages seem to be chosen in vindication of the use of the phylactery itself, as the reader will see on consulting them: Bind them for a Sign upon thy Hand - and for Frontlets between thy Eyes - write them upon the Posts of thy House, and upon thy Gates; all which commands the Jews took in the most literal sense. <div eID="gen38265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38266" type="x-p"/> Even the phylactery became an important appendage to a Pharisee's character, insomuch that some of them wore them very broad, either that they might have the more written on them, or that, the characters being larger, they might be the more visible, and that they might hereby acquire greater esteem among the common people, as being more than ordinarily religious. For the same reason, they wore the fringes of their garments of an unusual length. Moses had commanded (<reference osisRef="Num.15.38">Num 15:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.15.39">Num 15:39</reference>) the children of Israel to put fringes to the borders of their garments, that, when they looked upon even these distinct threads, they might remember, not only the law in general, but also the very minutiae, or smaller parts of all the precepts, rites, and ceremonies, belonging to it. As these hypocrites were destitute of all the life and power of religion within, they endeavored to supply its place by phylacteries and fringes without.
