But as Christ had to deal with the worst of hypocrites, who not only were swelled with proud contempt of <hi type="italic">God, </hi>and intoxicated with careless security, but had captivated the multitude by their enchantments, he found it necessary to exclaim against them with vehemence. He calls them <hi type="italic">serpents </hi>both in nature and in habits, and then threatens them with a punishment, which it will be in vain for them to attempt to escape, if they do not speedily repent.<div eID="gen101908" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101907" osisID="Matt.23.33" type="section"/>
entries.22ab69459995d1028954dad0519d0f70fd137a32: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.34" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.23.34" sID="gen101909" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">34.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore, lo, I send to you. Luke </hi>introduces it in a still more emphatic manner, <hi type="italic">Wherefore also the Wisdom of God hath said; </hi>which some commentators explain thus: “I, who am the eternal <hi type="italic">Wisdom of God, </hi>declare this concerning you.” But I am more inclined to believe that, according to the ordinary custom of Scripture, God is here represented as speaking in the person of his <hi type="italic">Wisdom; </hi>so that the meaning is, <hi type="italic">“God </hi>foretold long ago, by the prophetic Spirit, what would happen with regard to you.” This sentence, I acknowledge, is nowhere to be found literally: but as God denounces the incorrigible obstinacy of that people in many places of Scripture, Christ draws up a kind of summary of them, and by this personification <note n="111"> <div sID="gen101911" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En introduisant la Sapience de Dieu parlant</foreign>;” — “by introducing the Wisdom of God as speaking.”<div eID="gen101911" type="x-p"/> </note> expresses more clearly what was the judgment of God as to the incurable wickedness of that nation. For if those teachers would have no success, it might have appeared strange that Christ should have desired them to weary themselves to no purpose. Men argue thus: “God labors in vain, when he sends his word to the reprobate, who, he knows, will continue obstinate.” And hypocrites, as if it were sufficient of itself to have preachers of the heavenly doctrine continually with them, though they show themselves to be disobedient, entertain the conviction that God is reconciled and favorable to them, provided that the outward word be heard amongst them.<div eID="gen101910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101912" type="x-p"/>Thus the Jews fiercely boasted that, in comparison of other nations, they had always enjoyed the best <hi type="italic">prophets </hi>and teachers, and, as if they had deserved so great an honor, they considered this to be an undoubted proof of their own excellence. <note n="112"> <div sID="gen101913" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme un certain tesmoignage qu’ils estoyent gens de bien</foreign>;” — “as an undoubted proof that they were good people.”<div eID="gen101913" type="x-p"/> </note> To put down this foolish boasting, Christ not only affirms that they do not excel other nations on the ground of having received from God distinguished prophets and expounders of <hi type="italic">his Wisdom, </hi>but maintains that this ilk requited favor is a greater reproach, and will bring upon them a heavier condemnation, because the purpose of God was different from what they supposed, namely, to render them more inexcusable, and to bring their wicked malice to the highest pitch; as if he had said, “Though prophets have been appointed to you by heaven in close succession, it is idly and foolishly that you claim this as an honor; for God had quite a different object in his secret judgment, which was, to lay open, by an uninterrupted succession of gracious invitations, your wicked obstinacy, and, on your being convicted of it, to involve the children in the same condemnation with the fathers.”<div eID="gen101912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101914" type="x-p"/>With regard to the words, the discourse as related by Matthew is defective, but its meaning must be supplied from the words of Luke. The mention of <hi type="italic">scribes and wise men </hi>along with <hi type="italic">prophets </hi>tends to magnify the grace of God; by which their ingratitude becomes more apparent, since, though God left nothing undone for their instruction, they made no proficiency. Instead of <hi type="italic">wise men </hi>and <hi type="italic">scribes, Luke </hi>mentions <hi type="italic">apostles, </hi>but the meaning is the same. This passage shows that God does not always bestow salvation on men when he sends his word to them, but that he sometimes intends to have it proclaimed to the reprobate, who, he knows, will continue obstinate, that it may be to them<div eID="gen101914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101915" type="x-p"/>the savior of death unto death, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.2.16">2 Corinthians 2:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen101915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101916" type="x-p"/>The word of God, indeed, in itself and by its own nature, brings salvation, and invites all men indiscriminately to the hope of eternal life; but as all are not inwardly drawn, and as God does not pierce the ears of ally—in short, as they are not renewed to repentance or bent to obedience, those who reject the word of God render it, by their unbelief, deadly and destructive.<div eID="gen101916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101917" type="x-p"/>While God foresees that this will be the result, he purposely sends his prophets to them, that he may involve the reprobate in severer condemnation, as is more fully explained by Isaiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.6.10">6:10</reference>.) This, I acknowledge, is very far from being agreeable to the reason of the flesh, as we see that unholy despisers of God seize on it as a plausible excuse for barking, that God, like some cruel tyrant, takes pleasure in inflicting more severe punishment on men whom, without any expectation of advantage, he knowingly and willingly hardens more and more. But by such examples God exercises the modesty of believers. Let us maintain such sobriety as to tremble and adore what exceeds our senses. Those who say, that God’s foreknowledge does not hinder unbelievers from being saved, foolishly make use of an idle defense for excusing God. I admit that the reprobate, in bringing death upon themselves, have no intention of doing what God foresaw would happen, and therefore that the fault of their perishing cannot be ascribed to His foreknowledge; but I assert that it is improper to employ this sophistry in defending the justice of God, because it may be immediately objected that it lies with God to make them repent, for the gift of faith and repentance is in his power.<div eID="gen101917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101918" type="x-p"/>We shall next be met by this objection, What is the reason why <hi type="italic">God, </hi>by a fixed and deliberate purpose, appoints the light of his word to blind men? When they have been devoted to eternal death, why is he not satisfied with their simple ruin? and why does he wish that they should perish twice or three times? There is nothing left for us but to ascribe glory to the <hi type="italic">judgments of God, </hi>by exclaiming with Paul, that they are a deep and unfathomable abyss, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.11.33">Romans 11:33</reference>.) But it is asked, How does he declare that the prophecies will turn to the destruction of the Jews, while his adoption still continued to be in force towards that nation? I reply, As but a small portion embraced the word by faith for salvation, this passage relates to the greater number or the whole body; as Isaiah, after having predicted the general destruction of the nation, is commanded<div eID="gen101918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101919" type="x-p"/>to seal the law of God among the disciples, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.16">Isaiah 8:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen101919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101920" type="x-p"/>Let us know then that, wherever the Scripture denounces eternal death against the Jews, it excepts a <hi type="italic">remnant, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.11.5">Romans 11:5</reference>;) that is, those in whom the Lord <hi type="italic">preserves some seed</hi> on account of his free <hi type="italic">election</hi><div eID="gen101920" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.34" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101909" osisID="Matt.23.34" type="section"/>
entries.e42d86bf3aeb91aab09cf8e8817d2df354285c6e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.35" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.23.35" sID="gen101921" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">35.</hi> <hi type="italic">That upon you may come. </hi>He not only takes away from them their false boasting, but shows that they had received <hi type="italic">prophets </hi>for a totally different purpose, that no age might be free from the criminality of wicked rebellion; for the pronoun <hi type="italic">you</hi> embraces generally the whole nation from its very commencement. If it be objected, that it is not consistent with the judgment of God that punishment should be inflicted on the children for the sins of the parents, the answer is easy. Since they are all involved in a wicked conspiracy, we ought not to think it strange if God, in punishing all without reserve, make the punishment due to the fathers to fall upon the children. Justly then is the whole nation — in whatever age individuals may have lived — called to account, and likewise punished, for this unceasing contempt. For as God, by an uninterrupted course of patience, has unceasingly contended with the malice of the whole people, so the whole people is justly held guilty of the inflexible obstinacy which continued to the very last; and as every age had conspired to put to death its own <hi type="italic">prophets, </hi>so it is right that a general sentence should be pronounced upon them, and that all the murders, which have been perpetrated with one consent, should be avenged on all.<div eID="gen101922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101923" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">From the blood of Abel. </hi>Though <hi type="italic">Abel </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.8">Genesis 4:8</reference>) was not slain by the Jews, yet the murder of <hi type="italic">Abel </hi>is imputed to them by Christ, because there is an affinity of wickedness between them and Cain; otherwise there would have been no propriety in saying that <hi type="italic">righteous blood </hi>had been shed by that <hi type="italic">nation from the beginning of the world. </hi>Cain is therefore declared to be the head, and leader, and instigator of the Jewish people, because, ever since they began to slay <hi type="italic">prophets, </hi>they succeeded in the room of him whose imitators they were.<div eID="gen101923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101924" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To the blood of Zechariah. </hi>He does not speak of <hi type="italic">Zechariah </hi>as the latest martyr; for the Jews did not then put an end to the murder of the <hi type="italic">prophets, </hi>but, on the contrary, their insolence and madness increased from that period; and posterity, who followed them, satiated themselves with the blood which their fathers only tasted. Nor is it because his death was better known, though it is recorded in Scripture. But there is another reason, which, though it deserves attention, has escaped the notice of commentators; in consequence of which they have not only fallen into a mistake, but have likewise involved their readers in a troublesome question. We might suppose it to have arisen from forgetfulness on the part of Christ, that, while he mentions one ancient murder, he passes by a prodigious slaughter which afterwards took place under Manasseh. For until the Jews were carried to Babylon, their wicked persecutions of holy men did not cease; and even while they were still under affliction, we know with what cruelty and rage they pursued Jeremiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.32.2">32:2</reference>.) But our Lord on purpose abstains from reproaching them with recent murders, and selects this murder, which was more ancient—which was also the commencement and source of base licentiousness, and afterwards led them to break out into unbounded cruelty—because it was more suitable to his design. For I have lately explained, that his leading object was to show that this nation, as it did not desist from impiety, must be held guilty of all the murders which had been perpetrated during a long period. Not only, therefore, does he denounce the punishment of their present cruelty, but says that they must be called to account for the murder of <hi type="italic">Zechariah, </hi>as if their own hands had been imbrued in his blood.<div eID="gen101924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101925" type="x-p"/>There is no probability in the opinion of those who refer this passage to that <hi type="italic">Zechariah </hi>who exhorted the people, after their return from the Babylonish captivity, to build the temple, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Zech.8.9">Zechariah 8:9</reference>,) and whose prophecies are still in existence. For though the title of the book informs us that he was the son of Barachiah, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Zech.1.1">Zechariah 1:1</reference>,) yet we nowhere read that he was slain; and it is, forced exposition to say, that he was slain during the period that intervened <hi type="italic">between </hi>the building of <hi type="italic">the altar and of the temple. </hi>But as to the other <hi type="italic">Zechariah, </hi>son of Jehoiada, the sacred history relates what agrees perfectly with this passage; that when true religion had fallen into decay, after the death of his father, through the wicked revolt of the king and of the people, <hi type="italic">the Spirit of God came upon him, </hi>to reprove severely the public idolatry, and that on this account he was stoned in the porch of the temple, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.20 Bible:2Chr.24.21">2 Chronicles 24:20, 21</reference>.) There is no absurdity in supposing that his father Jehoiada received, in token of respect, the surname of <hi type="italic">Barachiah, </hi>because, having throughout his whole life defended the true worship, he might justly be pronounced to be the <hi type="italic">Blessed of God. </hi>But whether Jehoiada had two names, or whether (as Jerome thinks) there is a mistake in the word, there can be no doubt as to the fact, that Christ refers to that impious stoning of Zechariah which is recorded in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.21 Bible:2Chr.24.22">2 Chronicles 24:21, 22</reference><div eID="gen101925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101926" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Whom you slew between the temple and the altar. </hi>The crime is rendered still more heinous by the circumstance of the place, since they did not revere the sacredness of <hi type="italic">the temple. </hi>Here <hi type="italic">the temple </hi>is put for the outer court, as in other passages. Near it was the <hi type="italic">altar of burnt offerings,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.64 Bible:1Kgs.18.30">1 Kings 8:64; 18:30</reference>,) so that the priest offered the sacrifices in presence of the people. It is evident, therefore, that there must have been furious rage, when the sight of <hi type="italic">the altar and of the temple </hi>could not restrain the <hi type="italic">Jews </hi>from profaning that sacred place by a detestable murder.<div eID="gen101926" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101921" osisID="Matt.23.35" type="section"/>
entries.a87b41ca57c1cacb542732ccb5b430dd4c56541e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.23.37" sID="gen101927" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37.</hi> <hi type="italic">Jerusalem, Jerusalem. </hi>By these words, Christ shows more clearly what good reason he had for indignation, that <hi type="italic">Jerusalem, </hi>which God had chosen to be his sacred, and — as we might say — heavenly abode, not only had shown itself to be unworthy of so great an honor, but, as if it had been a den of robbers, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.11">Jeremiah 7:11</reference>,) had been long accustomed to suck the blood of the prophets. Christ therefore utters a pathetic exclamation at a sight so monstrous, as that the holy city of God should have arrived at such a pitch of madness, that it had long endeavored to extinguish the saving doctrine of God by shedding <hi type="italic">the blood of the prophets. </hi>This is also implied in the repetition of the name, because impiety so monstrous and incredible deserves no ordinary detestation.<div eID="gen101928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101929" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Thou who killest the prophets. </hi>Christ does not reproach them with merely one or another murder, but says that this custom was so deeply rooted, that the city did not care to slay every one of <hi type="italic">the prophets </hi>that were sent to it. For the participle, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀποκτείνουσα τοὺς προφήτας</foreign>), (<hi type="italic">killing</hi> <hi type="italic">the prophets,) </hi>is put for an epithet; as if Christ had said, “Thou who oughtest to have been a faithful guardian of the word of God, a teacher of heavenly wisdom, the light of the world, the fountain of sound doctrine, the seat of divine worship, a pattern of faith and obedience, art a murderer of <hi type="italic">the prophets, </hi>so that thou hast acquired a certain habit of sucking their blood.” <note n="113"> <div sID="gen101930" type="x-p"/> "<foreign xml:lang="fr">En sorte que tu est toute accoustoumee a humer leur sang, sans en faire conscience</foreign>;" — "so that thou art quite accustomed to suck their blood, without any scruple of conscience."<div eID="gen101930" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence it is evident, that they who had so basely profaned the sanctuary of God deserved every kind of reproaches. Yet Christ had likewise the intention to obviate the scandal which soon after arose, that believers, when they saw him basely put to death at Jerusalem, might not be confounded by the novelty of such an exhibition. For by these words they were already warned that it was not wonderful if a city, which had been accustomed to strangle or stone <hi type="italic">the prophets, </hi>should cruelly put to death its own Redeemer. This shows us what value we should attach to places. There never certainly was a city in the world on which God bestowed such magnificent titles, or such distinguished honor; and yet we see how deeply it was sunk by its ingratitude.<div eID="gen101929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101931" type="x-p"/>Let the Pope now compare the abode of his robbery with that holy city; what will he find worthy of equal honor? His hired flatterers boast to us that the faith flourished there in ancient times. But admitting this to be true, if it is evident that it has now, by wicked rebellion, revolted from Christ, and is full of innumerable deeds of sacrilege, what folly is it in them to maintain that the honor of primacy belongs to it? Let us, on the contrary, learn from this memorable example, that when any place has been exalted by uncommon instances of the favor of God, and thus has been removed from the ordinary rank, if it degenerate, it will not only be stripped of its ornaments, but will become so much the more hateful and detestable, because it has basely profaned the glow of God by staining the beauty of his favors.<div eID="gen101931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101932" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">How often would I have gathered together thy children. </hi>This is expressive of indignation rather than of compassion. The city itself, indeed, over which he had lately wept, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.19.41">Luke 19:41</reference>,) is still an object of his compassion; but towards the scribes, who were the authors of its destruction, he uses harshness and severity, as they deserved. And yet he does not spare the rest, who were all guilty of approving and partaking of the same crime, but, including all in the same condemnation, he inveighs chiefly against the leaders themselves, who were the cause of all the evils. We must now observe the vehemence of the discourse. If in <hi type="italic">Jerusalem </hi>the grace of God had been merely rejected, there would have been inexcusable ingratitude; but since God attempted to draw the Jews to himself by mild and gentle methods, and gained nothing by such kindness, the criminality of such haughty disdain was far more aggravated. There was likewise added unconquerable obstinacy; for not once and again did God <hi type="italic">wish to gather them together, </hi>but, by constant and uninterrupted advances, he sent to them <hi type="italic">the prophets, </hi>one after another, almost all of whom were rejected by the great body of the people.<div eID="gen101932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101933" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As a hen collecteth her brood under her wings. </hi>We now perceive the reason why Christ, speaking in the person of God, compares himself to <hi type="italic">a hen. </hi>It is to inflict deeper disgrace on this wicked nation, which had treated with disdain invitations so gentle, and proceeding from more than maternal kindness. It is an amazing and unparalleled instance of love, that he did not disdain to stoop to those blandishments, by which he might tame rebels into subjection. A reproof nearly similar is employed by Moses, that God, like<div eID="gen101933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101934" type="x-p"/>an eagle with outspread wings, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.11">Deuteronomy 32:11</reference>,)<div eID="gen101934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101935" type="x-p"/>embraced that people. And though in more than one way God <hi type="italic">spread out his wings </hi>to cherish that people, yet this form of expression is applied by Christ, in a peculiar manner, to one class, namely, that <hi type="italic">prophets </hi>were sent to <hi type="italic">gather together </hi>the wandering and dispersed into the bosom of God. By this he means that, whenever the word of God is exhibited to us, he opens his bosom to us with maternal kindness, and, not satisfied with this, condescends to the humble affection of <hi type="italic">a hen </hi>watching over her <hi type="italic">chickens. </hi>Hence it follows, that our obstinacy is truly monstrous, if we do not permit him to <hi type="italic">gather us together. </hi>And, indeed, if we consider, on the one hand, the dreadful majesty of God, and, on the other, our mean and low condition, we cannot but be ashamed and astonished at such amazing goodness. For what object can God have in view in abasing himself so low on our account? When he compares himself to a mother, he descends very far below his glory; how much more when he takes the form of <hi type="italic">a hen, </hi>and deigns to treat us as his <hi type="italic">chickens?</hi><div eID="gen101935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101936" type="x-p"/>Besides, if this charge was justly brought against the ancient people, who lived under the Law, it is far more applicable to us. For though the statement—which I quoted a little ago from Moses—was always true, and though the complaints which we find in Isaiah are just, that<div eID="gen101936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101937" type="x-p"/>in vain did God spread out his hands every day to embrace a hard-hearted and rebellious people, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.2">Isaiah 65:2</reference>)<div eID="gen101937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101938" type="x-p"/>that, though he rose up early, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.13">Jeremiah 7:13</reference>) he gained nothing by his incessant care of them; yet now, with far greater familiarity and kindness, he invites us to himself by his Son. And, therefore, whenever he exhibits to us the doctrine of the Gospel, dreadful vengeance awaits us, if we do not quietly hide ourselves under his wings, by which he is ready to receive and shelter us. Christ teaches us, at the same time, that all enjoy safety and rest who, by the obedience of faith, are <hi type="italic">gathered together </hi>to God; because <hi type="italic">under his wings </hi>they have an impregnable refuge. <note n="114"> <div sID="gen101939" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Un refuge quine peut faillir, et contre lequel il n’y a point de puissance qui ait lieu</foreign>;” — “a refuge which cannot fail, and against which no power can succeed.”<div eID="gen101939" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen101938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101940" type="x-p"/>We must attend likewise to the other part of this accusation, that God, notwithstanding the obstinate rebellion of his ancient people, was not all at once so much offended by it, as to lay aside a father’s love and a mother’s anxiety, since he did not cease to send <hi type="italic">prophets </hi>after <hi type="italic">prophets </hi>in uninterrupted succession; as in our own day, though he has experienced a marvelous depravity in the world, he still continues to dispense his grace. But these words contain still deeper instruction, namely, that the Jews, as soon as the Lord <hi type="italic">gathered them together, </hi>immediately left him. Hence came dispersions so frequent, that they scarcely remained at rest for a single moment <hi type="italic">under the wings </hi>of God, as we see in the present day a certain wildness in the world, which has indeed existed in all ages; and, therefore, it is necessary that God should recall to himself those who are wandering and going astray. But this is the crowning point of desperate and final depravity, when men obstinately reject the goodness of God, and refuse to come <hi type="italic">under his wings.</hi><div eID="gen101940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101941" type="x-p"/>I said formerly that Christ speaks here in the person of God, and my meaning is, that this discourse belongs properly to his eternal Godhead; for he does not now speak of what he began to do since he was manifested in the flesh, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Tim.3.16">1 Timothy 3:16</reference>,) but of the care which he exercised about the salvation of his people from the beginning. Now we know that the Church was governed by God in such a manner that Christ, as the Eternal Wisdom of God, presided over it. In this sense Paul says, not that God the Father was tempted in the wilderness, but that Christ himself was tempted, <note n="115"> <div sID="gen101942" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais que Christ luy-mesme a esté tenté au desert par le peuple deliveré d’Egypte</foreign>;” — “but that Christ himself was tempted in the wildrness by the people that had been delivered from Egypt.”<div eID="gen101942" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.9">1 Corinthians 10:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen101941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101943" type="x-p"/>Again, when the sophists seize on this passage, to prove free will, and to set aside the secret predestination of God, the answer is easy. “God <hi type="italic">wills </hi>to gather all men,” say they; “and therefore all are at liberty to come, and their <hi type="italic">will </hi>does not depend on the election of God.” I reply: The <hi type="italic">will </hi>of God, which is here mentioned, must be judged from the result. For since by his word he calls all men indiscriminately to salvation, and since the end of preaching is, that all should betake themselves to his guardianship and protection, it may justly be said that he <hi type="italic">wills </hi>to gather all to himself. It is not, therefore, the secret purpose of God, but his <hi type="italic">will, </hi>which is manifested by the nature of the word, that is here described; for, undoubtedly, whomsoever he efficaciously <hi type="italic">wills </hi>to <hi type="italic">gather, </hi>he inwardly draws by his Spirit, and does not merely invite by the outward voice of man.<div eID="gen101943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101944" type="x-p"/>If it be objected, that it is absurd to suppose the existence of two <hi type="italic">wills </hi>in God, I reply, we fully believe that his <hi type="italic">will </hi>is simple and one; but as our minds do not fathom the deep abyss of secret election, in accommodation to the capacity of our weakness, the <hi type="italic">will </hi>of God is exhibited to us in two ways. And I am astonished at the obstinacy of some people, who, when in many passages of Scripture they meet with that figure of speech <note n="116"> <div sID="gen101945" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Anthropopathie;</hi> c’est, quand Dieu s’attribue des affections semblables à celles des hommes, comme quand il dit</foreign> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.6">Genesis 6:6</reference>) <foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">qu’il s’est repenti d’avoir fait l’homme;</hi> et semblables passages</foreign>.” — “<hi type="italic">Anthropopathy;</hi> that is, when God ascribes to himself feelings similar to those of men, as when he says (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.6">Genesis 6:6</reference>) that <hi type="italic">he repented of having made man;</hi> and similar passages.”<div eID="gen101945" type="x-p"/> </note> (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀνθρωποπάθεια</foreign>) which attributes to God human feelings, take no offense, but in this case alone refuse to admit it. But as I have elsewhere treated this subject fully, that I may not be unnecessarily tedious, I only state briefly that, whenever the doctrine, which is the standard of union, <note n="117"> <div sID="gen101946" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">De vraye union</foreign>;” — “of true union.”<div eID="gen101946" type="x-p"/> </note> is brought forward, God <hi type="italic">wills </hi>to <hi type="italic">gather </hi>all, that all who do not come may be inexcusable.<div eID="gen101944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101947" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And you would not. </hi>This may be supposed to refer to the whole nation, as well as to the <hi type="italic">scribes; </hi>but I rather interpret it in reference to the latter, by whom the <hi type="italic">gathering together,</hi> <note n="118"> <div sID="gen101948" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ce rassemblement et ceste reunion</foreign>;” — “this gathering together and this union.”<div eID="gen101948" type="x-p"/> </note> was chiefly prevented. For it was against them that Christ inveighed throughout the whole of the passage; and now, after having addressed <hi type="italic">Jerusalem </hi>in the singular number, it appears not without reason that he immediately used the plural number. There is an emphatic contrast between God’s <hi type="italic">willing </hi>and their <hi type="italic">not willing;</hi> <note n="119"> <div sID="gen101949" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Quand ildit, <hi type="italic">Dieu a voulu, vous ne l’avez point voulu</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">;</hi>” — “when he says, <hi type="italic">God would, you would not.</hi>”<div eID="gen101949" type="x-p"/> </note> for it expresses the diabolical rage of men, who do not hesitate to contradict God.<div eID="gen101947" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101927" osisID="Matt.23.37" type="section"/>
entries.05d52f194232237980a3e47f74d39dade1ea0449: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.38" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.23.38" sID="gen101950" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">38</hi> <hi type="italic"> Lo,</hi> <hi type="italic">your house is left to you desolate. </hi>He threatens the destruction of the temple, and the dissolution of the whole frame of civil government. Though they were disfigured by irreligion, crimes, and every kind of infamy, yet they were so blinded by a foolish confidence in the temple, and its outward service, that they thought that God was bound to them; and this was the shield which they had always at hand: “What? Could God depart from that place which he has chosen to be his only habitation in the world? And since he dwells in the midst of us, we must one day be restored.” In short, they looked upon the temple as their invincible fortress, as if they dwelt in the bosom of God. But Christ maintains that it is in vain for them to boast of the presence of God, whom they had driven away by their crimes, and, by calling it <hi type="italic">their house, (lo, your house</hi> <hi type="italic">is left to you,) </hi>he indirectly intimates to them that it is no longer <hi type="italic">the house of God. </hi>The temple had indeed been built on the condition, that at the coming of Christ it would cease to be the abode and residence of Deity; but it would have remained as a remarkable demonstration of the continued grace of God, if its destruction had not been occasioned by the wickedness of the people. It was therefore a dreadful vengeance of God, that the place which Himself had so magnificently adorned was not only forsaken by Him, and ordered to be razed to the foundation, but consigned to the lowest infamy to the end of the world. Let the Romanists now go, and let them proceed, in opposition to the will of God, to build their Tower of Babylon, while they see that the temple of God, which had been built by his authority and at his command, was laid low on account of the crimes of the people.<div eID="gen101951" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.38" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101950" osisID="Matt.23.38" type="section"/>
entries.1c1bb2886ae2e8f44858a8876dfda2cf970f2c82: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.39" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.23.39" sID="gen101952" type="section"/> <div sID="gen101953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">39.</hi> <hi type="italic">For I tell you. </hi>He confirms what he had said about the approaching vengeance of God, by saying that the only method of avoiding destruction will be taken from them. For that was <hi type="italic">the accepted time, the day of salvation, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.8">Isaiah 49:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.6.2">2 Corinthians 6:2</reference>,) so long as that very person who had come to be their Redeemer, attested and proclaimed the redemption which he had brought. But at his departure, as at the setting of the sun, the light of life vanished; and therefore this dreadful calamity, which he threatens, must of necessity fall upon them.<div eID="gen101953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101954" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Until you say. </hi>We come now to inquire what period is denoted by this phrase. Some restrict it to the last day of judgment. Others think that it is a prediction, which was soon afterwards fulfilled, when some of the Jews humbly adored Christ. But I do not approve of either of these interpretations. And I am certainly astonished that learned men should have stumbled at so small an obstacle, by taking great pains to inquire how unbelievers can say concerning Christ, <hi type="italic">Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord; </hi>for he does not declare what they will be, but what he himself will do. And even the adverb <hi type="italic">until </hi>extends no farther than to the time which goes before. Joseph did not know his wife <hi type="italic">until </hi>she brought forth Christ, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.25">Matthew 1:25</reference>.) By these words Scripture does not mean, that after Christ had been born they lived together as husband and wife, but only shows that Mary, before the birth of her son, was a virgin that had not known man.<div eID="gen101954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101955" type="x-p"/>So then the true meaning of the present passage, in nay opinion, is this: <hi type="italic">“Hitherto </hi>I have lived among you in humility and kindness, and have discharged the office of a teacher; and no having finished the course of my calling, I shall depart, and it will not be possible for you any longer to enjoy my presence, but him whom you now despise as a Redeemer and a minister of salvation, you will find to be your Judge.” In this manner the passage agrees with the words of Zechariah, <hi type="italic">They shall look on him whom they pierced, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:Zech.12.10">Zechariah 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:John.19.37">John 19:37</reference>.) But Christ appears also to make an indirect allusion to their vain hypocrisy, because, as if they ardently longed for the promised salvation, they sung daily the words of the psalm,<div eID="gen101955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101956" type="x-p"/>Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord, <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.118.26">Psalm 118:26</reference>;)<div eID="gen101956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen101957" type="x-p"/>while they treated with scorn the Redeemer that was offered to them. In short, he declares that he will not come to them <hi type="italic">until, </hi>trembling at the sight of his dreadful majesty, they shall exclaim—when it is too late—that truly he is the Son of God. And this threatening is addressed to all despisers of the Gospel, more especially to those who falsely profess his name, while they reject his doctrine; for they will one day acknowledge that they cannot escape the hands of him whom they now mock by their hypocritical pretensions. For the same song is now sung by the Papists, who, after all, care nothing about Christ, <hi type="italic">until, </hi>armed with vengeance, he ascends his tribunal. We are also reminded, that so long as Christ exhibits himself to us in the name of the Father as the herald of salvation and Mediator, we ought not only to honor him with our lips, but sincerely to wish that he would make us and the whole world subject to himself.<div eID="gen101957" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.23.39" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen101952" osisID="Matt.23.39" type="section"/>

entries.3f47ef5a1f21399e6824588bce482cc749f76d75:

               <ns0:head>CHAP. XXIII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p>THen spake Jesus to the multitude, and to his disciples.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Saying, the scribes, and the Pharisees sit in Moses seat.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 All therefore whatsoever they bid you ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> observe and do: but do not ye after their works, for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 2.21.22.</ns0:note> they say, and do not.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Lord having now done with the <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> turneth his D<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>scourse to the more Docible People, who (as we heard be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore) heard him attentively, and gladly, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 12.37. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 19.48. Our Saviour fore-saw, that some unwary Hear<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers might make two ill uses of what he had spoke against the <ns0:hi>Scribes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>isees.</ns0:hi> 1. Some might report him an Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />my to the Law t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e Interpreters of which the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> were. 2. Others mig<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t contemn the Authority of the Law, because he had represented these Men, in whose Hand the Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tat<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>on of it at present, was so truly Contemptible. Whereas on the other side, many might run into Errors of Practice, from the Example of the <ns0:hi>Scribes,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> their Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gistrates and Teachers. Against all these mistakes, he Cau<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions them in this <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> Shewing, that he did not under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />value the Law of Moses, nor would have his Reflections on the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> prejudice any thing which they taught them of it, and according to it; neither would he have his People take the Copy of the Law from their Actions. <ns0:hi>The Scribes, and Pharisees sit in Moses seat.</ns0:hi> These Men were the or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary <ns0:hi>Readers,</ns0:hi> and Interpreters of the Law of God. <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> is here put for the Law, as <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 16.31. <ns0:hi>If they hear not Moses,</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> and so <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 29. <ns0:hi>They have Moses and the Prophets. Moses</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Seat</ns0:hi> signifieth the <ns0:hi>Seat</ns0:hi> appointed for those, that gave the Sense of the Law, or Judgment up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on it, thus <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 15.21. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 3.15. <ns0:hi>Moses in old time, hath in every City those that Preach him, being Read in the Synagogue every Sabbath Day.</ns0:hi> Their way was, while they Read the Scriptures, they <ns0:hi>Stood up,</ns0:hi> (paying a particular Reverence to the pure Word of God) <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 4.16. when they had done Reading, they <ns0:hi>sate down and opened it.</ns0:hi> Their sit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting in the Seat of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> did not signifie a <ns0:hi>Succession</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> for he had no Successor, being the <ns0:hi>Mediator</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Old Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stament.</ns0:hi> But the delivering and interpreting the Doctrine, and <ns0:hi>Law of M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ses.</ns0:hi> Dr. <ns0:hi>Lightfoot</ns0:hi> thinks it is rather to be understood of the <ns0:hi>Chair of M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>gistracy,</ns0:hi> than the <ns0:hi>Doctrinal Chair.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Phar sees</ns0:hi> being Exercised in that, it may be understood of both, for the Reading, and Interpreting the Law, chiefly belong'd to the <ns0:hi>Scribes. All therefore whatsoe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver they bid you observe, observe and do.</ns0:hi> That is, whatsoe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver is in <ns0:hi>M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ses,</ns0:hi> which they bid you observe, and do. The Term <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi> is to be understood restrainedly, with respect to the Subject, matter or Persons spoken of, in Multitudes of Scriptures. OurSaviours cautioning his Disciples, so often against the <ns0:hi>Leaven</ns0:hi> of these Men, and their <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> plainly sheweth us, that must be here the Sense of it. Let not the Law of God lose its Authority with you, because of these wicked Men. He doth not Command them to hear none but them, for then to what purpose did he himself Preach, or send out the Twelve, if none might hear them. All that can be concluded from this Text is, <ns0:hi>That the Law of God, or Word of God, is not to be dispised whoever Reads, or delivereth it,</ns0:hi> he goeth on. <ns0:hi>But after their Works do not, for they say and do not.</ns0:hi> We are Naturally more led by Example, than by Precept. Men had therefore need be Cautioned against ill living Teachers. <ns0:hi>Odi Philosophum qui non sapir sibi.</ns0:hi> A Man had need very well know the Medicine, which he taketh from a Physician, he seeth Sick of the same Disease, when he himself refuseth and Abominates it. He that <ns0:hi>sa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s and doth not,</ns0:hi> may be heard, but not imitated. There may be a time, when Men can ordinari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly hear no others, which was the present Case.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 6.13<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> For they bind heavy burdens, and grie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vous to be born, and lay <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> upon mens shoul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ders, but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour saith the same of the <ns0:hi>Lawyers, Luke</ns0:hi> 11.46. The <ns0:hi>Burdens</ns0:hi> here mentioned, were not their <ns0:hi>Traditions</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ritual things,</ns0:hi> Christ would never have before commanded his Disciples to <ns0:hi>observe</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>do them,</ns0:hi> but the things truly com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded <ns0:hi>by the Law of God,</ns0:hi> especially the <ns0:hi>Ceremonial Law,</ns0:hi> called a <ns0:hi>Yoke, Acts</ns0:hi> 15.10. which (say the Apostles) <ns0:hi>neither we nor our Fathers were able to bear.</ns0:hi> They are, saith our Saviour, Riged Exactors, aed Pressers of the Law of God, up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on others, but will not themselves use the least endeavours (such as the <ns0:hi>putting to of a Finger</ns0:hi>) themselves to do them. 1. He blameth them that their own Lives, no way answered their <ns0:hi>Doctrine.</ns0:hi> 2. It may be, he also blameth their too Ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ged pressing the Law in all the Minute things of it: There may be a too Rigorous Pressing of the Law. Good Teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers will be faithful in delivering the whole Counsel of God, yet Teaching no more than themselves will endeavour to pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctise, and being Conscious of Humane Infirmity, they will do it, with great Tenderness, and Compassion, joyning <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> both together.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6 <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 2, 5.16.</ns0:note> all their works they do for to be seen of men. They make broad their phylacteryes, and inlarge the borders of their garments.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour had <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. blamed the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> for not living up to what they taught, pressing the Law of God on others, but not doing nor indeavouring to observe it themselves. Here he blames them, for doing what good things they did for <ns0:hi>O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stentation,</ns0:hi> to be seen of Men, and abounding in their Ritual Performances of more minute Concernment, in the mean time neglecting their Moral Duties. <ns0:hi>All they do, they do to be seen of Men</ns0:hi>; this is their main end to be seen of Men; for this he had reflected on them, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6. <ns0:hi>They make broad their Phylacteryes, and inlarge the borders of their Gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments.</ns0:hi> For the right understanding of this we must have recourse to <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 15.37, 38. <ns0:hi>And the Lord spake unto Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses, saying, spake unto the Children of Israel, and bid them that they make them Fringes in the Borders of their Gar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments, throughout their Generations, And that they put up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the Fringe of the Borders, a Ribband of Blew; And it shall be unto you for a Fringe, that you may look upon it, and remember all the Commandements of the Lord, and do them, and that you seek not after your own Heart, and your own Eyes, after which you use to go a Whoring. That you may remember, and do all my Commandments.</ns0:hi> Deut, 22.12. <ns0:hi>Thou shalt make thee Fringes upon the four Quarters of thy Vesture, wherewith thou coverest thy self.</ns0:hi> In obedience to this Law, the Jews did generally wear such Garments that had <ns0:hi>Fringes,</ns0:hi> and Blew <ns0:hi>Ribbands</ns0:hi> annexed to them. The Jews at this Day do it not, because, as they pretend, they have lost the true way of <ns0:hi>Dying</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Blew Colour,</ns0:hi> required in the Law. The End why God commanded them, is expressed. <ns0:hi>That they might look upon it, and remember all the Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandements of the Lord and do them,</ns0:hi> and be restrained from their own Inventions, and Imaginations in Gods Service. They were also a Note of Distinction of the Jews from other Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, Besides these, God Commanding that they should Bind his Laws, <ns0:hi>for a Sign upon their Hands, and as frontlets be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween their Eyes, Deut.</ns0:hi> 6.6, 7, 8. they made them <ns0:hi>Parch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments,</ns0:hi> in which the Precepts of the Law were written, which they bound to their <ns0:hi>Foreheads,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Arms.</ns0:hi> These were cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led <ns0:hi>Phylacteryes</ns0:hi> from <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to keep. Things wherein the Law was kept, the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> for a Boast how zealous keep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers they were of the Law of God (than which they did no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing less) made these <ns0:hi>Phylacteries</ns0:hi> and Ribbands broader, their <ns0:hi>Fringes</ns0:hi> much longer than other Mens, this is that ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />king broad their <ns0:hi>Phylacteryes,</ns0:hi> and inlarging the Borders of their Garments, which our Lord here reflects upon, done only for <ns0:hi>Ostentation,</ns0:hi> and that they might be seen of Men.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
